verdict: Caution: lend selectively to value-added Kochi spice processors with proven export order books and tight working-capital control; avoid pure commodity traders and thinly-capitalised bulk exporters until unit-level data is collected.
title: Kochi Spices Processing & Trade: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
Spices processing in Kochi is a working-capital business wearing a factory coat. You buy raw cardamom, pepper, chilli and coriander in the February-to-June arrival window, hold stock, clean/sort/grind/blend, and sell into domestic FMCG or export. **Cash is trapped in inventory and receivables, not in the plant.** ICRA flags net working capital over operating income of around 45% as on March 31, 2025, improved from 51% in FY2024, with seasonal raw-material availability (February to June) forcing higher stock [9]. So when a proposal lands, check the stock-and-debtor cycle month by month, not the annual balance sheet; if inventory days spike outside the procurement window, ask why.

## Where value and cash sit now
Value sits in branded/value-added product, not bulk. Orkla India's Q1 FY27 revenue rose 10.4% with pricing contributing 11.4%, as chilli and coriander inflation climbed 78% and 40% respectively [6]. **Processors with brand and pricing power pass inflation through; bulk traders absorb it.** Peer Orkla's Q3 FY26 spices volumes surged over 10% with EBITDA up 17.7% [4], and its international business is around 21% of revenues across 45 countries [5]. Rating reports note utilisation peaks July-to-November, typically till Diwali [10]. So when a proposal lands, check whether the borrower's margin is pricing-led or volume-led; if margin is flat while raw material is inflating, ask for the customer-wise price revision letters.

## What has changed
Kerala's first FTA consignment to New Zealand was flagged off from Kochi by Synthite Industries, with the India-New Zealand agreement in force from October 20 [1]. That is a real new-market opening for established exporters. Against it, India-wide exports are down 5.7% Apr-to-date in USD [D], and bank credit is growing 26.3% YoY against output of 5.1% [D] — **credit is running far ahead of output, so lending standards, not demand, are the risk.** Kerala GST collections are up 10.3% Apr-to-date versus India's 6.1% [D], a genuine local tailwind. The Kochi spice conference in February 2026 flagged regulatory shifts and traceability as priorities [3]; treat that as a compliance-cost signal, not a demand signal.

## Who to pursue, who to avoid
Pursue value-added processors and grinders with branded or private-label domestic customers, documented export order books (FTA-linked or Gulf), and a demonstrated pass-through record. Avoid pure commodity traders, single-buyer bulk exporters, and anyone whose growth is funded by credit rather than orders. **The FTA story belongs to firms already exporting; do not underwrite a first-time exporter on it.**

## How to grow safely
Structure as cash-flow lending against stock and receivables with a drawing-power formula, not a clean term loan. Take monthly stock statements, ageing of debtors, and GST returns; covenant a maximum inventory-to-sales ratio and a minimum export realisation percentage. Rating reports show a peer servicing around Rs 54 crore of repayments and Rs 15-20 crore capex in FY2027 from cash flows [10] — **size repayments to the trough of the seasonal cycle, not the peak.** Collect from customer: actual inventory days, debtor days, and buyer concentration for each proposal.

## Early-warning signs
- Monthly stock statement (monthly): inventory days rising outside February-June procurement -> ask for ageing and slow-moving stock write-down.
- GST returns vs sales (monthly): GST turnover falling below book sales -> stop fresh disbursement and reconcile.
- Export realisation (monthly): realisation percentage dropping or buyer concentration rising -> seek additional collateral or reduce limit.
- Raw material price index (monthly): chilli/coriander inflation not matched by price revisions -> review margin covenant.
